note.note:
Consult Summary:
- 26-year-old male with known asthma presenting with acute chest tightness, wheeze, and nonproductive cough after a recent upper respiratory tract infection; reported symptom onset ~3 hours prior to consult and has been without his inhalers for ~1 week.

History:
- Presenting complaint:
  - Acute chest tightness described as inability to take a full breath; onset approximately 3 hours prior to consultation.
  - Associated wheeze and persistent nonproductive cough.
  - Recent viral-type illness last week with sore throat and runny nose; those symptoms improving but cough and wheeze persisting.
- Timeline/progression:
  - Cold last week; runny nose and sore throat improving.
  - Cough and wheeze persisted following the cold.
  - New/worse chest tightness began about 3 hours before the consult.
- Exacerbating/relieving factors:
  - Symptoms slightly worse at night.
  - Increased shortness of breath with exertion (walking up stairs).
  - Not short of breath at rest (patient report).
  - Patient has been without inhalers for approximately one week (ran out while away at university).
- Associated symptoms/systems review:
  - Sore throat and runny nose (recent, improving).
  - No sputum production.
  - No chest pain per patient (tightness only).
- Pertinent negatives:
  - No current shortness of breath at rest.
  - No sputum production.
  - No drug allergies reported.

Past Medical History:
- Asthma: long-standing since childhood; prior severe exacerbation requiring intubation and inpatient stay at age ~16–17.
- Allergic rhinitis/hay fever.
- Childhood eczema.
- Childhood milk protein allergy.

Medications:
- Salbutamol (Ventolin) inhaler — dose/route/frequency not documented; patient reports he has used it but is currently out of medication.
- Clenil / Clenil Modulite (beclometasone inhaler) — dose/route/frequency not documented; patient currently out of medication.
- Spacer: patient believes he "has one somewhere"; clinician will send a new spacer.
- Oral steroid tablets prescribed for 5 days: "two tablets in the morning" stated; steroid name and tablet strength/dose not documented.
- Allergies: no known drug allergies; environmental allergies to dust reported.

Social History:
- Student: was away at university last week (forgot/ran out of inhalers while away).
- Smoking, alcohol, and recreational drug use: not documented in the transcript.
- No other social/financial/lifestyle details documented.

Family History:
- Mother: eczema.
- Father: asthma.

Physical Examination:
- No vital signs documented.
- No physical examination findings documented during the consult.

Investigations:
- No investigations or test results documented.
- No peak flow recorded (patient did not have one).

Assessment & Plan:
- Issue 1: Acute asthma exacerbation (likely triggered by recent viral upper respiratory infection)
  - Assessment: Patient with known asthma, wheeze, cough, chest tightness; symptomatic deterioration after recent URTI; out of inhaler therapy for ~1 week.
  - Plan:
    - Prescribe reliever inhaler (Salbutamol / Ventolin) — dose/route/frequency to be provided on prescription (dose/route/frequency not documented in transcript).
    - Prescribe maintenance inhaler (Clenil / Clenil Modulite) — dose/route/frequency to be provided on prescription (dose/route/frequency not documented in transcript).
    - Prescribe oral corticosteroid course for 5 days; clinician stated "two tablets in the morning" — steroid name and tablet strength not documented.
    - Provide spacer device and instructions for use; clinician will send a new spacer with usage instructions.
    - Advise Clenil as ongoing maintenance (e.g., morning) and Ventolin as needed (PRN).
    - Safety-netting: seek medical attention if Ventolin use required more frequently than every 3 hours, or if symptoms worsen (worsening shortness of breath, increased chest tightness or pain, light-headedness).
    - Prescriptions to be sent; clinician anticipated they could be available within an hour.
- Issue 2: Recent upper respiratory tract infection contributing to symptoms
  - Assessment: Cold last week with residual cough and sore throat; likely viral trigger for wheeze/asthma symptoms.
  - Plan:
    - Symptomatic management and asthma treatment as above.
    - Rest recommended.
- Issue 3: Lack of current inhaler access / recent nonadherence due to running out of medications
  - Assessment: Patient ran out of both inhalers ~1 week ago while at university.
  - Plan:
    - Immediate prescription of inhalers and spacer to restore inhaler access.
    - Advice to use spacer to improve inhaler delivery.
    - Recommend follow-up with GP or asthma review once symptoms settle to ensure ongoing supply and review inhaler technique / adherence.

General Plan items:
- Provide time off work as appropriate; patient can self-certify for first seven days (clinician noted likely to provide time off / advised rest).
- Discussed steroid side effects (mood changes, hyperglycemia, rash, nausea, headache); patient instructed to read medication labels and monitor for adverse effects.
- Safety-netting reiterated: seek urgent care for worsening symptoms at any time.

Quality checks (document_quality):
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - No vital signs recorded.
  - No physical examination documented (respiratory auscultation, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation).
  - No peak expiratory flow measurement.
  - Specific medication names given but dose, route, and frequency not documented for inhalers or oral steroid (steroid name/strength not documented).
  - No smoking, alcohol, or substance-use history recorded.
  - No plan for follow-up appointment or specific timeframe for reassessment documented.
- Internal conflicts from the transcript:
  - None identified; patient initially stated he uses inhalers, later clarified he has run out and does not have them currently.
- Transcript quality:
  - Overall understandable; one brief instance of minor audio cutting out during the clinician explanation but did not prevent extraction of key clinical information.
